Chapter 12 — The Salt Road

March 3, 2026 by P. Navarre

The flats began where the last of the olive trees gave up, and Kestrel walked into them at the hour when the light goes flat and colourless, when even the shadows seem uncertain of themselves.

She had been told the crossing took four days. She had been told this by a man who had never crossed it, in a room that smelled of wet wool and cheap anise, and she had believed him because believing him was cheaper than staying.

Salt crusted the ground in plates the size of dinner tables. Where the plates met, they had buckled upward into low ridges, and walking meant choosing between the ridges and the powder, and the powder was worse.

Nothing crosses the flats twice.
Not water. Not birds. Not debts.

By the second evening she had stopped counting her steps and started counting her swallows of water instead, which was a worse game, because it had an ending she could see coming.

II

The thing about the salt, Kestrel decided, was that it did not care. Rock cared, in its way — rock would turn an ankle, would send scree down at you, would at least acknowledge that you were there. The salt simply continued in all directions and let you do whatever you were going to do.

On the third day she found the cart. It had been there a long time. The wood had gone grey and then gone soft, and the iron had bled orange stains down into the crust beneath it, so that the whole thing sat in a faint rusty halo like a saint in a bad fresco.

Translator's note: the idiom here is closer to "like a saint painted by someone who owed money."

She did not look inside it. She told herself this was because there was no time, and she kept telling herself that for the rest of the crossing, and mostly it worked.
